name: Assyrian Neo-Aramaic
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand descriptions agree (3 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: In Assyrian, stress is expiratory and normally is placed on the penultimate. It is not shifted in verb suffixation (i.e. is goes to the newly formed penultimate). Stress often affects the quality and length of vowels; it may cause the ommission of vowels and, at times, of entire syllables. (Tsereteli 1978)

new_statements.rule_in_words: In words of more than one syllable stress falls on the penultimate syllable (the 'canonical position'); the stress domain includes S-suffixes (stress moves to the new penult) but not L-suffixes, the -va suffix or the enclitic copula and particles da/ze (stress stays on the penult of the base); final stress only in monosyllables and a few forms such as 3pl -e; loanwords are adapted to penultimate stress; some particles have antepenultimate stress (kedamta 'in the morning').
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 129 snippet: compound place names of Azeri/Persian origin (Gurcustan, Ermenistan) carry a secondary stress on the first component, 'interpreted as reflecting their status as stress groups'; no general secondary-stress rule visible in the snippets (search-inside q=secondary stress returned only this hit).
new_statements.exceptions: monosyllables and 3pl suffix -e (final stress, p. 143); reduced demonstratives such as +avvo < +avvoha with final stress after elision (p. 226); words with epenthetic /e/ showing stress two syllables from the end at the surface (p. 206); particles kedamta, morisa, +berasa, laxxane with antepenultimate stress (p. 231); L-suffixes, va-suffix and enclitics (copula, da, ze) outside the stress domain (pp. 228, 232); imperatives and numerals per the compilers snippet notes (pp. 229, 235) not re-read here.
new_statements.identity_note: Khan 2016 describes the Christian Neo-Aramaic dialect of Urmi (C. Urmi, north-western Iran), the variety underlying the Assyrian literary koine; the catalog entry 'Assyrian Neo-Aramaic' (assy1241) covers this dialect.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In words of more than one syllable, stress falls on the penultimate syllable (the 'canonical position'); it is largely predictable but marked in transcription because of some variation. Deviations are grammatically/lexically conditioned: loanwords with source-final stress are adapted to penultimate (+sárbaz < Pers. sarbáz, p. 227); in verbs stress counts S-suffixes and is regularly penultimate but does not move onto L-suffixes or the va suffix (p. 228); imperatives stress the initial syllable regardless of length (p. 229); some particles/adverbials retract to the antepenult (kédamta, móriša, p. 231); vocatives may take antepenultimate stress (p. 227); the copula and inclusive particles da/zə are enclitic and leave stress on the penult of the base word (bétan-ilə, p. 232); polysyllabic numerals take final stress (p. 235); final stress otherwise only in monosyllables and a few forms like 3pl -é (p. 143).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only mention seen (p. 129, snippet): Azeri-origin place names in -stan behave as stress groups, primary stress on the first component with an optional secondary stress (grave accent) on the suffix, e.g. Gürcüstàn; no general secondary-stress rule visible in the snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: monosyllables and 3pl suffix -é (final); imperatives (initial); certain particles/adverbials and vocatives (antepenult); polysyllabic numerals (final); L-suffixes/va suffix not counted for verb stress; enclitic copula and da/zə outside the stress domain; stress-group phenomena (numeral+noun, negator+verb, demonstrative+noun, quantifier cúl-) where only one word bears stress (sec. 1.19, p. 234-237); occasional stress shift when two verbal forms are closely linked (p. 234).
new_statements.identity_note: Khan 2016 describes the Christian Urmi dialect (C. Urmi) of North-Eastern Neo-Aramaic, i.e. the variety on which literary Assyrian Neo-Aramaic is based; statements are for that dialect, not for all NENA dialects grouped under assy1241.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: Maclean 1895 sect. 8 p.13 statement found verbatim in the scanned text we hold; Stoddard 1855:20 corroboration downloaded and confirmed; Noeldeke 1868 sect. 30 downloaded and agrees (second-hand from Stoddard); open-access NENA volumes we hold and Coghill 2020 give only family-level 'penultimate unless marked' notes. Every source seen agrees that default word stress is penultimate, so the penultimate stress is not in doubt and nothing suggests a reclassify of the position. The weakness is vintage and kind: the classification rests on a database entry (StressTyp2 < Tsereteli 1978, unverified) checked against an 1895 missionary reference grammar, while a 2016 four-volume reference grammar of the same dialect (Khan, Urmi) and a 1988 phonology monograph (Odisho) exist and are not yet obtained. Maclean's own sect. 8 (5)-(7) and Stoddard already record affix/enclitic-conditioned antepenult and some oxy
